# Letter of Jeremiah — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Unknown; pseudonymously attributed to the prophet Jeremiah |
| **Date** | c. 300–100 BCE; Greek papyrus fragment found at Qumran dated c. 100 BCE |
| **Audience** | Jews in Babylon or under Hellenistic influence facing pressure to participate in idol cult |
| **Genre** | Satirical polemical epistle / anti-idolatry sermon |
| **Timeline** | Fictional setting: eve of the Babylonian exile (6th century BCE) |
| **In One Sentence** | A brilliantly repetitive satirical letter, ostensibly written by Jeremiah to Jews about to be deported to Babylon, demolishes the pretensions of idol worship with vivid, sometimes darkly comic, evidence that idols are utterly helpless — and closes each round of argument with the same emphatic refrain: therefore they are obviously not gods. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Letter of Jeremiah is one of the most unusual texts in all of deuterocanonical literature — unusual in its form (an actual letter, or something shaped like one), in its strategy (relentless repetition as a literary device rather than a flaw), and in its tone (satirical contempt that tips occasionally into something approaching comedy). To understand it, one must understand the specific situation it addresses: Jewish communities living in polytheistic urban environments where public religious life was inseparable from the worship of gods made of wood, stone, silver, and gold.

The problem of idolatry in the Diaspora was not theoretical. For a Jew living in Babylon, in Alexandria, in Antioch, or in any major Hellenistic city, the cult of local gods was woven into every aspect of public life: civic festivals, market days, political ceremonies, military victories, funerals, and weddings all involved rituals honoring statues of gods. Guild memberships, trade relationships, neighborhood associations — all of these came with implicit or explicit expectations of participation in communal sacrifices and festivals. The question was not simply theological (are these idols real gods?) but practical and social (what happens to us if we refuse to honor them?).

The fictional frame of the letter — Jeremiah writing to the exiles as they are about to be deported to Babylon — is drawn from the actual letter Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Jeremiah 29. In that letter, Jeremiah told the deportees to "seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile" (Jer 29:7) — an instruction to accommodate to some degree in their environment. The Letter of Jeremiah is, in a sense, the counter-instruction: accommodate in some ways, yes, but never in this particular way. When you see the Babylonians carrying their gods in procession and the nations falling down before them, remember what you know. These are not gods. Here is the evidence. Do not be afraid of them.

The Qumran Greek papyrus of the Letter of Jeremiah — designated 7Q2 — is the oldest surviving fragment of any deuterocanonical text ever found, dating to approximately 100 BCE. Its presence at Qumran indicates that the letter was in circulation among the sectarian Jewish communities of the Dead Sea region, far from any Babylonian urban environment, which suggests it was read not only as practical guidance for city-dwelling Diaspora Jews but as a general theological affirmation of Jewish distinctiveness.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The book has a single, focused purpose: to inoculate its readers against the appeal of idol worship by making idols look ridiculous. The author's method is not primarily philosophical — the argument is not that idols cannot logically be divine — but observational: look at what these things actually are and what they actually do (and fail to do), and you will see that they are obviously not gods.

The argument proceeds in approximately ten rounds, each developing a different aspect of idol helplessness, and each closed with a variant of the refrain: "From this you will know that they are not gods; do not fear them." The rounds cover the following territory: idols cannot speak, cannot move, cannot protect themselves from thieves or birds, cannot set up a king or remove one, cannot grant rain or judge a case, cannot be distinguished from a corpse, rot and are eaten by insects, are dressed by priests and handled by women who are ritually unclean, burn up in fires set around them. The cumulative effect is of a list that keeps growing until the object under examination has been thoroughly stripped of any possible pretension to divinity.

The author may have been responding specifically to the theatrical grandeur of Babylonian and then Hellenistic religious processions, in which divine statues were carried through the streets on litters and in palanquins with great ceremony, attended by priests in elaborate dress, surrounded by music and incense and cheering crowds. To an outsider with no template for interpreting the spectacle, the display would have been impressive — perhaps intimidatingly so. The author's strategy is to deflate it: that enormous statue being carried through the streets cannot walk, so it must be carried. The priests who carry it spend more on their own food than they contribute to it. The women who dress it are menstruating. Strip away the ceremony and what you have is a piece of wood or metal being moved from place to place by people who are, at best, employed and, at worst, deceiving themselves.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Letter of Jeremiah is short enough to read in fifteen minutes, but its distinctive structure rewards attention rather than mere rapid consumption. The refrain — "From this you will know that they are not gods; do not fear them" (or close variations) — appears ten or eleven times in the seventy-three verses, dividing the text into clearly demarcated sections. The first encounter with the refrain is straightforwardly declarative. By the fifth or sixth repetition it has become almost a drumbeat — insistent, cumulative, almost liturgical in its rhythm. By the final repetition the reader who has been paying attention finds it genuinely stirring: after all this evidence, after all these demonstrations of idol helplessness, the refrain is not a desperate rhetorical attempt to close a weak argument but the confident conclusion of a thorough case.

The humor in the text deserves recognition. The observation that bats, swallows, and birds land on the idols' heads, and cats walk across their bodies (v. 22), is genuinely funny — and deliberately so. The detail that the priests steal from the offerings to give to their concubines (v. 9–10) punctures clerical pretension with sharp economy. The comparison of idols to a scarecrow in a cucumber garden (v. 70) is one of the most deflating analogies in ancient polemical literature. The author knows that contempt is a powerful weapon against reverence, and laughter breaks the spell of awe that idols depend on for their social power.

This is a text designed to be heard in community — repeated aloud, ideally in a context where the community in question was under real pressure to accommodate idol worship. The repetition that irritates a solitary reader scanning the page would have worked differently in an oral context: each repetition of the refrain would have drawn the gathered community into a shared declaration, a communal insistence on what they knew and refused to forget. Reading it this way — as a text for public delivery, not private study — unlocks its rhetorical logic.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

**Jeremiah 10:1–16 (the idolatry polemic it elaborates):** The Letter of Jeremiah is, in many ways, an extended dramatization of Jeremiah 10:1–16, which contains one of the Hebrew Bible's most concentrated anti-idolatry arguments: "A tree from the forest is cut down... they decorate it with silver and gold; they fasten it with hammer and nails so that it cannot move. Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field" (Jer 10:3–5). The Letter of Jeremiah takes these images and multiplies them across seventy-three verses. The scarecrow comparison in v. 70 is almost certainly a direct echo of Jeremiah 10:5.

**Jeremiah 29 (the letter to the exiles):** The real Letter of Jeremiah, which gave the pseudepigraphical letter its frame, told the exiles to settle in Babylon, plant gardens, and seek the city's welfare. The Letter of Jeremiah in the deuterocanon can be read as the instruction that complements Jeremiah 29's accommodation: settle down, yes — but do not bow down.

**Isaiah 44:9–20 (craftsman's folly satire):** The great Deutero-Isaiah satire on idol-making — in which a man cuts a tree in half, uses one half for cooking and the other for making a god — is the most extended predecessor of the Letter of Jeremiah's argument. Both texts focus on the manufacturing process as itself a reductio ad absurdum: a god made by human hands is a made thing, and made things cannot be ultimate things. The Letter of Jeremiah adds texture and specificity but inherits its core argument from Isaiah 44.

**Wisdom of Solomon 13–15 (the philosophical elaboration):** Where the Letter of Jeremiah argues by comic inventory, the Wisdom of Solomon argues by philosophical analysis. Wisdom 13–15 traces the psychological and spiritual logic by which idolatry develops — starting from a relatively innocent admiration of nature, progressing through craftsman's vanity, arriving at morally destructive cult practice. Reading the two texts together reveals two complementary strategies for the same concern: the Letter of Jeremiah attacks through ridicule, the Wisdom of Solomon through analysis.

**Psalm 115 and Psalm 135 (the idol-has-eyes-but-cannot-see tradition):** The refrain psalms about idols — "They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see; ears, but do not hear" (Ps 115:5–6, 135:16–17) — are the liturgical ancestors of the Letter of Jeremiah's argument. The psalms make the point concisely and communally; the Letter of Jeremiah expands it into a full satirical catalogue. Together they show how consistent and persistent this particular strand of Jewish anti-idolatry theology was.

**Bel and the Dragon (Additions to Daniel):** Bel and the Dragon — one of the Additions to Daniel — takes the same anti-idolatry argument and dramatizes it as a detective story. Where the Letter of Jeremiah argues in the abstract that priests steal from the offerings, Bel and the Dragon shows Daniel actually exposing the priests who do exactly this. The two texts complement each other: the Letter of Jeremiah provides the theological argument; Bel and the Dragon provides the narrative demonstration.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The repetition that most modern readers find tedious is not a sign of weak composition. In both ancient Jewish and Greco-Roman rhetorical traditions, deliberate repetition — anaphora — was a recognized and respected device for building emphasis, creating rhythm, and driving a point home to an audience. The refrain of the Letter of Jeremiah works like the refrain of a psalm or a ballad: its power accumulates precisely because it keeps coming back. A modern reader skimming for new information at each return of the refrain is fighting against the text's own logic. The point is not that each section adds new information — though it does — but that the accumulation of the refrain changes its emotional and rhetorical weight with each repetition.

The gender dynamics of the text are worth attending to. The author's use of women ritually impure (v. 29–30) as an argument against idol credibility reflects the ritual purity categories of his culture in ways that modern readers find uncomfortable. The argument is: if this were truly a holy object, impure people would not be permitted near it or permitted to handle it. The argument is addressed to Jews who shared those purity categories; its force depends on shared assumptions. Modern readers need not endorse those assumptions to understand the argument's internal logic within its own cultural framework.

The text's relationship to Baruch is confusing in the manuscript tradition. In some textual traditions the Letter of Jeremiah circulates as Baruch chapter 6; in others it circulates as an independent text. The choice to include it in Baruch was editorial, not authorial — the original text had no connection to the Book of Baruch — but the placement made a certain theological sense: both books address the situation of exile and both take the threat of assimilation seriously. This project's decision to treat it as a standalone text (LJR) reflects the most historically accurate understanding of its origins.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Letter of Jeremiah is not in the Hebrew Tanakh because, like most deuterocanonical texts, it was composed in Greek (or at minimum its earliest surviving form is Greek) and circulated as a Greek text. The existence of the Qumran papyrus fragment (7Q2) indicates the text was in circulation by 100 BCE, but whether this fragment represents a translation from a Semitic original or is itself the original Greek is debated.

In the Latin tradition, the letter was commonly appended to the Book of Baruch as its sixth chapter, and it appears in this form in the Vulgate and in Catholic editions of the Bible today. The Council of Trent (1546) defined it as canonical within the deuterocanon, and it is included as Baruch 6 in Roman Catholic Bibles, as an independent text in Eastern Orthodox Bibles, and in the Apocrypha sections of editions like the New Revised Standard Version.

Protestant Bibles generally do not include it; when they do, it appears in the Apocrypha either as a standalone letter or appended to Baruch. Its short length (73 verses, one chapter) and its limited theological content compared to other deuterocanonical texts mean it has received relatively little attention in Protestant scholarship, though its importance as a document of Diaspora Jewish anti-idol polemic is significant for understanding the world in which early Christianity emerged.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 597 BCE | First Babylonian deportation of Judeans — the historical event the letter addresses |
| 586 BCE | Destruction of Jerusalem; second deportation — the book's narrative setting |
| c. 300–200 BCE | Most probable earliest date for the composition of the Letter of Jeremiah |
| c. 167–164 BCE | Maccabean revolt; anti-idolatry texts take on renewed urgency under Antiochus IV |
| c. 100 BCE | 7Q2 — Greek papyrus fragment of Letter of Jeremiah found at Qumran; oldest surviving deuterocanonical manuscript fragment |
| c. 100 BCE | Text in circulation in Greek Septuagint tradition |
| c. 200 CE | Letter of Jeremiah begins to circulate as "Baruch chapter 6" in some Latin traditions |
| c. 382–405 CE | Jerome's Vulgate appends Letter of Jeremiah to Baruch as chapter 6 |
| 1546 CE | Council of Trent defines the text (as Baruch 6) as deuterocanonical for Roman Catholics |
| 1611 CE | King James Bible includes the text in the Apocrypha, sometimes as a standalone letter |
